body: A drop this deep, alongside the first easing in input cost inflation for months, weakens the case for further Australian monetary tightening. That leaves the Australian dollar exposed if rate markets start pricing a gentler path. The sharp fall in new export orders also points to softening external demand, at a time when global equities are already under heavy pressure. Prices are still running above their long-run averages, though, so policymakers are unlikely to move quickly to declare inflation beaten. Traders may also treat the flash reading cautiously until the final data in early December. --- Higher interest rates are now hitting Australian demand across the board: services have joined manufacturing in contraction, new orders are at a five-year low and confidence is draining away. Australia's private sector shrank at its fastest pace in more than five years in November , according to flash survey data from S&P Global, as higher interest rates and softer demand at home and abroad hit both manufacturers and service providers. The flash composite output index fell to 46.1 from 48.2 in October. That is its lowest reading since August 2021 and the second straight month below the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The weakness was broad. The services business activity index dropped to 46.2 from 48.5, while the manufacturing PMI slipped to 48.7 from 49.6 and the manufacturing output index fell to 45.3 from 46.2. Services output declined at the sharpest rate in 36 months, and manufacturing output at the steepest in 25 months. Weak demand was the main driver. Total new orders fell for the first time in five months and at the fastest pace since August 2021, and services new business is now shrinking faster than manufacturing orders. Firms cited subdued economic conditions, tight budgets and higher borrowing costs. New export orders also fell at the sharpest rate in just over two years, as uncertainty in overseas markets weighed on foreign demand. With less new work coming in, businesses reduced their backlogs for the first time since June and cut staff for the second time in three months. Manufacturers shed jobs faster than service firms. Business confidence fell to a three-year low. There was some relief on prices. Input cost inflation eased for the first time in four months, even with higher fuel, transport, supplier and wage costs and a further marked lengthening of manufacturers' delivery times. Firms also raised their selling prices more slowly than in October. Both measures remain above their long-run averages. Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the easing in price pressures showed that the recent tightening in financial conditions was working. She cautioned, though, that falling employment and confidence point to weaker output ahead, while inflation has yet to be fully brought under control. body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. A run of agency reports this month has pushed expectations toward oversupply and weighed on crude. Brent crude was up 1.1% at $92.88 per barrel at 11:50 a.m. ET on Thursday, well below its October levels above 110 dollars but little changed from the start of the week, while WTI crude gained 1.7% to 84.69 dollars per barrel. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that the global oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recover faster than global demand. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, and the agency now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, a swing from its previous forecast of a 1.8 million bpd deficit. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3 million bpd from last month, cut its 2027 demand forecast by 80,000 bpd to 104.3 million bpd, and lowered the implied call on OPEC crude by 220,000 bpd to 20.8 million bpd. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has moved in the same direction . In October, it forecast a 700,000 bpd inventory draw in the fourth quarter. It now expects stocks to build in Q4 and to rise by an average of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027, after drawing down for most of this year. The EIA estimates that crude production shut in across the Gulf fell to 2.5 million bpd in October, from 4.8 million bpd in September and a peak of 10.9 million bpd in May. OPEC said crude output from the OPEC+ alliance rose by roughly 2 million bpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Related: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge Analysts at Standard Chartered caution that higher Gulf output does not yet mean more oil reaching buyers. Tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure and record freight rates are still holding back shipments, and inventories drained earlier this year have left little cushion. The bank also warns that the IEA’s surplus call is larger than any other agency’s, and that forecast surpluses in the past have often failed to arrive on schedule. The agencies also disagree on demand. OPEC’s November report puts global oil demand at 108.3 million bpd in 2027, almost 4 million bpd above the IEA’s figure, and keeps its forecast for 2027 demand growth at 2.55 million bpd. The two agencies measure liquids differently, so the gap overstates the disagreement, but it remains wide. The IEA expects petrochemical feedstocks to drive most of next year’s growth, with little increase in gasoline and diesel use. The EIA expects global liquids demand to grow by 2 million bpd in 2027 after falling by about the same amount this year. Standard Chartered says the demand question will decide how much of the returning Gulf supply the market can absorb. OPEC’s higher consumption forecast leaves room for far more barrels than the IEA’s. The bank expects continued attacks on shipping, maritime security risks and stalled talks to keep a geopolitical premium in prices and sustain volatility, but still sees crude prices falling through 2027 as the market slowly normalizes. In natural gas, Standard Chartered expects European prices to hold at elevated levels through winter, even if milder weather on the continent and better LNG supply bring short-term relief. Europe has already drawn heavily on storage that started the season low: EU gas inventories stood at 70.4% on Nov. 15, about 18 percentage points below the five-year average. In the decade since 2016, when LNG exports began, and crude oil shipments were allowed to go not only in Canada, U.S. energy exports have soared to make America one of the major crude oil exporters and the world’s biggest exporter of LNG, propane, and ethane. Over the past decade, the U.S. toppled Qatar and Australia to become the single largest LNG exporter, while it regularly exports more crude oil volumes than any of the OPEC producers except Saudi Arabia. The U.S. energy industry has beaten all oil and gas export records this year, as domestic production and capacity keep rising while supply from the Middle East collapsed in the wake of the Iran war. U.S. export volumes will continue rising in the coming years as LNG capacity expands, oil production hits record highs, and buyers prefer supply that doesn’t need to transit geopolitically sensitive chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Middle East. Related: U.S. Oil Drillers Pick Up the Pace Just as Oil Prices Fall But raising the market share would be more difficult to achieve, following a surge from a low base in the past decade that has made the U.S. a dominant supplier of LNG, oil, and fuels. Now the U.S. is competing with the top exporters of almost every major energy commodity, and further gains in market share will depend on demand and pricing, not only on geopolitical considerations. Since 2018, U.S. crude oil exports have jumped from up to 5% of global exports to up to 15% of total shipments, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire. In the LNG market, the U.S. has toppled Qatar and Australia from the top spots and is now the single largest exporter with a 30% global market share in recent months, up from just 5% in 2018. In the propane market, the U.S. dominates global exports with a record market share of 70% year to date, according to Kpler’s data crunched by Reuters. U.S. propane exports increased to 2 million barrels per day (bpd) in the first half of 2026, up by 11% from a year earlier, as the Iran war crippled the Middle East’s supply to India and other countries in South Asia, EIA data showed. But continued growth in propane exports could be constrained by export capacity limitations and drought conditions at the Panama Canal related to El Niño, the U.S. administration said last month. U.S. ethane exports hit a record high of 794,000 bpd in August, the latest available EIA dataset shows . Crude oil and petroleum product exports also hit all-time highs this year, as disruptions to international crude oil and refined product flows through the Strait of Hormuz increased global demand for U.S. exports. Energy exports are further set to increase in absolute volumes, but this may not translate into gains in market share as rival exporters are also raising capacities, and those hit by the Middle East crisis are adapting to what could be lasting changes in global energy trade flows. body: Gold surges as oil and natural gas prices tumble in mixed Monday trading Commodity prices were mixed on Monday, November 23, amid an extended a three-week losing streak, while and precious metals higher, based on Trading Economics prices as of 11am in Singapore. WTI Crude oil in the US dropped 40 cents to $83.007 per barrel while Brent dropped 60 cents to $91.963 per barrel. Oil prices fell on Monday amid a "selloff" in wider financial markets, driven by concerns over whether the AI sector can boost economic growth, spilled over into commodities. Asian equities opened lower on Monday (Nov. 23), including a 4% drop in South Korea. Continuing attacks on Gulf shipping limited the losses, and Brent fell 4% last week and WTI 5%. Natural gas: Trading Economics also showed natural gas down about 4%, though it was still up 8.33% over the past month. I found no specific reason for the drop. Gold: Reports show gold futures up between about 2% and 3% in recent sessions. I found no clear driver beyond the broader market selloff. Iran: One analyst noted that oil moved lower as Trump signaled there’s no rush on an Iran decision. Over the past month, crude has fallen 18.31%, but it’s still 41.28% above a year ago. The US Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) November outlook expected Brent to stay near $100 a barrel for the rest of the year, well above the 91.963 on your screen. The outlook says oil rose for a third consecutive month in October, citing tanker attacks in the Persian Gulf, tighter supply and higher shipping costs. Watch for any decision from Washington, further tanker attacks and a possible equity rebound. I couldn’t find reasons for the moves in wheat, soybeans, copper and coal. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has claimed that the sharp decline in oil prices following the November midterm elections vindicates his earlier predictions, describing the controversy surrounding energy prices as a “Giant Hoax”. In a social media post on Monday, November 23, Trump questioned the timing of the decline in oil prices, suggesting that the movement had happened as he had anticipated. “Isn’t it interesting that Oil prices have dropped precipitously after the Midterm Elections? I said that was going to happen,” Trump wrote. Trump's remarks appear aimed at countering criticism over energy costs, particularly the impact of oil and fuel prices on American households, businesses and the wider economy. Oil prices are politically sensitive in the US because changes in crude prices can influence gasoline, diesel, transportation and food costs. Energy prices also affect inflation expectations and consumer confidence, making them an important issue for voters. However, a decline in oil prices following an election does not, by itself, establish that the election caused the movement or that political predictions were responsible. Global crude prices are influenced by several factors, including supply and demand, OPEC+ production decisions, geopolitical developments, inventories, currency movements and expectations about economic growth. Trump's post puts oil prices back at the centre of the political debate, as the administration seeks to highlight falling energy costs as evidence of economic progress.

title: Could Another Fed Rate Hike Be A Policy Mistake? Bill Ackman Says 3% Inflation Target Is More Realistic - TradingView
body: The Federal Reserve is set to meet in December for its last policy decision of 2026, with markets overwhelmingly expecting a rate hike after policymakers raised concerns about rising inflation. However, some Wall Street experts, including Pershing Square Inc.’s (PS) Bill Ackman, believe that a hike would be a policy mistake under current circumstances. In a post on X, the activist investor said that he thinks the central bank is “about to make another mistake on December 9th” if it hikes interest rates under massively tightening financial conditions. body: Broadcom shares shed 12% on Friday as a broad selloff swept through AI chip stocks, leaving the stock at €277.80 — roughly 35% below its 52-week high. The retreat came as investors began questioning both the scale and the profitability of spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to Reuters, with AP reporting that chip names came under pressure on worries about AI expenditures and the pace of the infrastructure buildout. For holders of Broadcom stock, that shift in sentiment pushes a more specific question to the fore: how much profitable business can the company actually capture from all this spending? The answer will determine whether Friday's lower price marks an attractive entry point or simply reflects expectations for the AI business that have been marked down for good. Size alone doesn't settle the matter. Even if demand for AI infrastructure holds up, what counts for Broadcom is how much of that demand lands in its own order book — and how much margin comes with it. An outlook that merely points to rising demand would therefore carry less weight than one that addresses how the business tied to that demand is likely to develop. Analyst moves in the days before Friday's drop illustrate how the Street is balancing those two ideas. Goldman Sachs trimmed its price target to $460 from $540 on Wednesday while keeping its buy rating, citing lower valuation multiples among comparable companies. The firm now applies a multiple of 25 times earnings to Broadcom, down from the 30 times it had used previously. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Broadcom? TD Cowen also stayed at buy, though it lowered its target to $425 from $475. Rothschild & Co went further in the prior Friday's session, downgrading Broadcom to neutral from buy and cutting its target to $398 from $595. Buy ratings on their own, in other words, no longer signal that the houses put the same valuation on the shares as before. The more favorable scenario would see AI infrastructure investment remain substantial and Broadcom convert it into profitable growth. An outlook along those lines could ease the doubts that shaped Friday's trading. To make that case, the company need not promise any further acceleration in spending — what matters is that expected demand translates into a profitable business. The danger isn't confined to a possible slowdown in investment. Even with spending running high, Broadcom's slice of the business could prove less lucrative than anticipated. That is why the next hard data point carries weight: Broadcom has scheduled fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results for December 9, 2026. body: The Nasdaq dropped 10% this week, its worst showing since March 2020, while the S&P 500 and Dow entered corrections. body: ACE fell to about $0.0001 on BNB Chain but still traded around $0.04 on centralised exchanges, and traders exploited that gap until the bridge ran dry. The drained 53.7 million tokens are almost half of the roughly 116 million ACE in circulation before the attack. They now sit in 24 wallets, and one wallet alone holds 26.1 million, so the main near-term risk is selling pressure on exchange-listed ACE. Gate is moving its ACE perpetuals to reduce-only and then delisting them, which leaves one fewer place to hedge. The incident is too small to affect BTC, ETH, crypto equities or ETF flows. Its main significance is for how the market prices bridge risk in small-cap gaming tokens. One abused minter role let a hacker walk off with $2 million, and a crowd of opportunists took the next $3.7 million before the bridge ran out of tokens. An attacker exploited privileged minting access on blockchain gaming studio Fusionist's ACE bridge on Sunday, creating vast amounts of unbacked ACE on BNB Chain and selling them for about $2 million, according to an analysis of onchain data by The Block. Opportunistic traders then bought the near-worthless copies and redeemed them through the bridge for genuine tokens, stripping it of about 53.7 million ACE worth roughly $3.7 million. ACE is the native token of Endurance, the blockchain Fusionist runs to support its sci-fi strategy games, and it pays transaction fees on that network. A version of the token also lives on BNB Chain. The bridge between the two normally holds Endurance ACE as backing, so burning a BNB Chain token releases an equal amount on Endurance. That design held only as long as nobody could mint BNB Chain ACE without collateral. Onchain Lens said the attacker abused the bridge's minter role, and The Block found the mints came from a wallet funded by Fusionist's deployer almost three years ago. Security firm Blockaid, which first flagged the exploit, listed that wallet among the attacker's addresses. The minting began just before 1 p.m. US Eastern time with 3.5 million tokens and escalated over roughly two and a half hours, ending with a single mint of 10 quintillion ACE. Each batch was dumped into decentralised exchange pools as soon as it appeared, and the proceeds of about 1,150 ETH were moved to Ethereum and routed into the Tornado Cash mixer. The selling drove BNB Chain ACE to about $0.0001 while the token still fetched around $0.04 on centralised exchanges, and that gap is where the second loss came from. The Block traced one wallet that started with about $50, spent $10 testing the bridge and used the remaining $40 to buy roughly 404,000 ACE. The bridge released the same number of real tokens within minutes, and the trader sold them for about $17,670, a return of around 350 times, all in under 20 minutes. By Sunday afternoon the bridge held 0.08 ACE, and a further 27 redemption attempts totalling about 1.36 billion tokens failed for lack of reserves. Fusionist told users to pause ACE transfers, trading and bridging on BNB Chain while it investigated, but had issued no further update at the time of The Block's report. Gate said it would reverse all ACE/USDT trades from the first mint to 2:15 p.m. Eastern, leaving some sellers with negative balances, and moved its ACE perpetual futures to reduce-only ahead of a planned delisting. The incident adds to a long run of bridge failures in 2026 and shows how one compromised privilege can turn a contained theft into a public scramble. How Fusionist handles the tokens now sitting with the traders who drained it, and whether other exchanges follow Gate in unwinding trades, are the next questions for ACE holders. body: There were big losses today (Friday, Nov 20th) in the financial markets, and things could get a lot worse, very quickly. Major indexes were off sharply, with the Nasdaq down 5.28% and the S&P 500 down 3.70%. AI stocks were especially hard hit and have been dropping recently as investors question the extreme valuations in that sector. Cryptocurrencies, which reversed lower several weeks ago, accelerated their rate of decline as Bitcoin (-5.4%), Ethereum (-7.29%), and Ripple (-5.11%) all came close to setting new 52-week lows. (see Eggs Are Not Dairy, Crypto Is Not Money ) Gold and silver set the tone early in the week and continued the carnage today, with gold down 2.38% and silver down 3.83%. For the week, gold declined $400 oz, or 10%; and silver dropped from $49 oz to $41 oz, a decline of 20%. All of this is taking place concurrently with declining home sales (the lowest in sixteen years), a weak job market, and higher interest rates. (see Ex-Chair Powell True To His Word – Higher For Longer ) The popularity of various sectors (technology, artificial intelligence, etc.) and the size of specific big-cap stocks (Apple, Nvidia, Amazon, etc.) have become so extreme that major indexes rise and fall with the fortunes of just a few individual companies. Extreme popularity and valuations of startup technology companies in the late 1990s caused growth indices to significantly outpace nearly all other measures of stock market growth. When the inevitable market correction came, many of those “high tech” companies went out of business. Stock prices dropped so violently that the NASDAQ lost nearly 80%, declining from an intraday peak close to 5000 in February 2000, down to about 1100 in August 2002. Early this year, chipmaker stocks hit record highs. Until just recently, the obsession with AI had powered stocks and indexes to new record highs again. Is this sustainable? After this week’s action, we might think not. Also, early this year, gold and silver peaked and reversed. Gold is currently down 35% from its price of $5400 in January, and silver is down 66% from its January high at $120. (see Gold & Silver – A Matter Of Perspective ) Last year, Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies peaked dramatically, then reversed. Since the summer of 2025, Bitcoin is down 55%, Ethereum is down 68%, and Ripple is down 75%. Is this the end? No. But it might be the beginning of something very ugly. In that case, expect the very ugly part to last a very long time. body: Copper prices came under heavy selling pressure last week, with futures in New York and London tumbling in tandem to post their worst weekly performance in about 19 months. Waning confidence in the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom, combined with a persistently strong US dollar and rising expectations of Federal Reserve (Fed) tightening, prompted a rapid exit of capital from industrial metals, with copper becoming the core target of this wave of selling. The most actively traded December copper contract on the New York Commodity Exchange (COMEX) dipped intraday to $5.439 per pound (about NT$180) on Friday (the 20th) before closing down $0.1485, or 2.64%, at $5.485 per pound. Entering Asian trading hours on Monday of this week, LME three-month copper briefly broke below the $12,000 per ton mark, dipping to about $11,958.93 before recovering to around $12,240.50, up about 1% intraday. Note: The COMEX front-month contract's weekly decline was the largest since the week of August 1, 2025, and marked the sixth consecutive weekly loss; the LME weekly decline was the worst in about 19 months since early April 2025. Copper is widely used in power equipment, transmission and distribution networks, data centers, and industrial manufacturing. In recent years, it has benefited from AI infrastructure buildouts and energy transition demand, which provided significant support for prices. However, with tech stocks recently undergoing a sharp correction, investors have begun reassessing the pace of capital expenditure growth at major technology companies and whether related investments can continue to translate into actual metals demand, putting copper prices under pressure from simultaneous downward revisions to valuations and demand expectations. Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, noted that increasing signs suggest the AI investment boom is weakening, and the Federal Reserve may need to adopt more aggressive tightening measures to control inflation, while a stronger US dollar is further weighing on copper prices. He believes investors will closely watch US monetary policy developments, Chinese demand, and global trade flows as the basis for judging the market's future direction. The appreciation of the US dollar makes dollar-denominated commodities more expensive for buyers holding other currencies, creating additional pressure. Market participants believe that, beyond interest rate policy and US dollar trends, Chinese industrial demand, the global manufacturing outlook, and the pace of AI data center construction will be key indicators for whether copper prices can stabilize and halt their decline. title: ‘No use pretending otherwise’: Chalmers warns of tough year ahead as jobless and inflation forecasts worsen - SMH.com.au
body: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has pledged to produce “budget-sized” spending cuts to put downward pressure on inflation after revealing a bleak economic outlook far worse than expected, with unemployment on track to breach 5 per cent. As economists rate the chances of a local recession at up to fifty-fifty, Chalmers used an address to parliament to warn that the country faced “difficult times full of serious risks”, with economic growth to slip below 2 per cent for the next two years. Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese have been under fire over the state of both the economy and the budget, with inflation at 4.3 per cent, unemployment at a five-year-high and real wages falling – all while the budget is in deficit. The Reserve Bank has pushed official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, although financial markets now believe it will have to start cutting by September to help prop up the economy. Chalmers conceded the economy faced strong headwinds that households were already starting to feel. He said higher oil prices meant inflation was now likely to remain in the mid-threes until near the end of next year. Interest rates would also weigh on household spending. “This means GDP growth could slow from 2.3 per cent last year to well below 2 per cent for the next two years. Treasury expects unemployment to stay below pre-pandemic averages but now peak higher, above 5 per cent,” he said. “2026 has been a very tough year for our people, our economy and the world. No use pretending otherwise. Interest rates are biting, unemployment is rising, prices are going up, wages aren’t keeping pace and families are hurting.” All forecasts are worse than what Chalmers announced in his May budget. At the time, he forecast economic growth would slow to 1.75 per cent this year before recovering to 2.25 per cent in 2027-28, that inflation would average 2.5 per cent, and that the jobless rate would remain around 4.5 per cent. Economists with NAB on Monday said the outlook for the jobs market could be even worse, forecasting unemployment to reach 5.5 per cent early in 2028. At that level, the jobless rate would be at its highest level – outside of the pandemic – since 2018. In May, Chalmers forecast the budget would show a deficit of $31.5 billion this financial year, followed by shortfalls of $31 billion, $34.4 billion and $25.3 billion in the three following years. Tax as a share of the economy was forecast to reach 23.8 per cent, its highest point since the 2005-06 record of 24.2 per cent. Government spending as a share of the economy was expected to reach 26.8 per cent. Chalmers said in the short-term the budget deficit was likely to be a little smaller this year but deficits would likely be larger from 2027-28 onwards. The economy is already a little smaller than anticipated, which meant tax and spending as a share of GDP were likely to be slightly higher, even with savings in the mid-year update. title: Trump's Economic Policies Fuel Inflation Fears As Wall Street Faces Growing Risk of Major Sell-Off - تسنیم
body: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, which posted gains through much of 2026 on strong corporate earnings and enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, have both entered correction territory, falling more than 10% from their recent highs. The latest economic indicators offer little reassurance to investors, with inflation accelerating in September and further price increases expected in the coming months. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% year over year in September, up from 3.4% in August and reaching its highest level since May. Research from the Federal Reserve Banks of St. Louis and Minneapolis indicates that Trump's tariffs were the main driver of inflation earlier in the year, while energy-related supply disruptions have since become the dominant factor. The war on Iran has disrupted oil shipments from the Middle East, driving up crude prices and transportation costs and adding further pressure to an already strained economy. The outlook remains troubling. The Cleveland Federal Reserve estimates that headline inflation could reach 3.9% in November, while core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is projected to climb to 2.9%, up from 2.6% in September. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September for the first time in three years. Persistent inflation has fueled expectations of another increase in December. Higher borrowing costs could further undermine consumers and businesses, slow economic growth and squeeze corporate profits, adding to pressure on an already vulnerable stock market. The S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio reached 40.1 in October, marking its sixth consecutive month above 40. The last time the index recorded comparable valuations was during the dot-com crash in September 2000. Historical data from Robert Shiller and YCharts shows that when the CAPE ratio exceeded 40, the S&P 500 delivered an average return of zero over the following six months, lost an average of 3% over one year and declined by an average of 19% over two years. Although the CAPE ratio does not account for future earnings growth and artificial intelligence could support corporate profitability, the figures highlight the risks associated with exceptionally expensive stocks. The historical comparisons also reflect overlapping periods during the dot-com bubble and should not be treated as definitive forecasts. Nevertheless, the combination of persistent inflation, potentially higher interest rates and elevated stock valuations presents a serious threat to Wall Street. Trump's economic agenda, already associated with tariff-driven price pressures, now faces another test as investors confront the possibility of a deeper market downturn.

For background, the S&P Global's flash US Purchasing Managers' Indexes for manufacturing and services are released at 9:45 am ET, typically about a week before the end of the month. Based on roughly 85% of the month's survey responses, they're among the first indicators of US business conditions for the current month. Final readings follow in the first few business days of the next month and usually differ only slightly from the flash. The PMIs are diffusion indexes drawn from monthly surveys of senior purchasing executives at private-sector companies. Readings above 50 point to expansion from the previous month and readings below 50 to contraction. The manufacturing PMI is a weighted composite of new orders, output, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of purchases. The services PMI headline is the business activity index, based on a single question about the volume of activity compared with the prior month. A composite output index combines manufacturing output and services activity into one gauge of private-sector growth. The details often matter more than the headlines. Input prices and prices charged are closely watched as early signals of inflation, showing how much cost pressure firms are facing and how much they're passing on to customers. New orders, backlogs, employment and business expectations give an early read on demand and hiring, and the report's commentary frequently highlights the impact of tariffs, supply chains and policy uncertainty. The S&P Global PMIs usually carry less weight with markets than the ISM surveys, which have longer track records and a larger following, and the two don't always agree. Their edge is timing and global comparability. Flash PMIs for the eurozone, UK, Japan, Australia and India are released the same day, letting traders compare US momentum with other major economies. He currently runs his own company,… The energy transition is often described as a switch from one extraction industry to another. Instead of digging up coal and drilling for oil, the argument goes, we will simply dig up enormous quantities of lithium, copper and nickel. There is some truth in that description. More mines will be needed for several important metals. But it misses the much larger change taking place underneath. A renewable and electrified energy system can require substantially less ongoing extraction than the fossil system it replaces. The world can need more copper mines while needing less mining for energy overall. That is good news for the environment. For companies and communities built around moving more fossil fuel ever, it is a warning. The transition is not necessarily replacing their product with an equally large market for another material. It is changing how much material the energy system needs to consume. A 2023 analysis in Joule by Joey Nijnens, Paul Behrens, Oscar Kraan, Benjamin Sprecher and René Kleijn puts the comparison into perspective. Coal accounted for 97% of the starting extraction mass in their modeled energy-system comparison. This is not 97% of all mining worldwide. Using an IEA net-zero pathway, they estimated that ore extraction associated with EV batteries would grow 55-fold from 2021 levels, compared with 13-fold for solar and ninefold for wind. Yet combined energy-related ore and coal extraction in 2040 remained well below 2021 coal extraction alone, including sensitivities for declining ore grades and different recycling rates. Crucially, the researchers translated refined mineral requirements into ore extraction. They were not simply comparing tonnes of battery metal with tonnes of coal while ignoring the rock processed to obtain those metals. It is also not a complete inventory of every construction material or every tonne of earth disturbed worldwide. The authors’ accompanying explanation describes a reduction approaching half relative to 2021 coal extraction, even with rapid clean-energy expansion. That is the missing denominator in many arguments about a mining explosion. But this is a scenario, not an automatic outcome. The economic difference is straightforward. Fossil fuels must be extracted repeatedly because their useful energy is released by consuming them. Every replacement shipment supports another round of production, transport and combustion. Copper in a cable performs a different function. It helps deliver electricity for decades without being consumed as fuel. Some of that copper can subsequently be recovered and used again. According to Yahoo Finance, S&P 500 futures rose 4% and Nasdaq 100 futures rallied 6% before the opening bell, after both indexes fell sharply on Friday. Early Monday, Reuters reported that doubts over the ability of the artificial intelligence sector to boost economic growth had "spilled over into commodities" after the AI selloff hit global markets, and crude added to a three-week losing streak. Reuters attributed Monday's decline to increased Middle East flows and the restart of Libya's Sharara pipeline. The chairman of Libya's National Oil Corporation said crude had begun flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, hours after the state firm warned that the pipeline closure would cut about 350,000 barrels per day from output. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that global oil supply has surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran, and it expects a surplus in the fourth quarter. JPMorgan expects persistent oversupply to hold Brent in the high $70s in the first half of 2027. "Oil recorded its third successive weekly loss, with pressure coming primarily from the supply side of the equation," PVM analyst Tamas Varga said, according to Reuters. President Donald Trump appeared to give diplomacy more time , Bloomberg reported, after he told Fox News that U.S. strikes could resume against Iran after the New Year if the two sides fail to reach a deal. Weekend attacks failed to lift prices. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they launched missiles and drones at U.S. military positions in Bahrain, and Yemen's Houthis claimed a direct hit on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery, a claim Saudi authorities had not confirmed as of Monday morning. Kpler data cited by Reuters columnist Ron Bousso show oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 9.5 million barrels per day in the 10 days to November 19, down from 12.2 million bpd in October. body: ConocoPhillips to Exit Norway in $4.43 Billion Deal with Vaar Energi Ukrainian naval drones sank a Russian warship in the Libyan port of Benghazi, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, in Kyiv's first admitted strike on Libyan soil and the latest attack along the Mediterranean route that carries Russian oil to Asia. According to Zelenskiy, the seven drones sank the corvette Merkury, destroyed a Ka-27 helicopter along with it and hit the Russian dry cargo ship Angara, a vessel Moscow used to transport weapons. The strike followed a drone attack that set the Russian military-linked cargo ship Sparta II ablaze in the Gulf of Finland. Finland's military says Ukraine likely carried out the attack, while Kyiv has not claimed responsibility as of early Monday. The Merkury, a Project 20380 corvette commissioned in 2023, had docked in Benghazi to refuel and resupply while escorting Russian cargo ships, according to the Institute for the Study of War. Libya's eastern-based government in Benghazi, which is aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army has ties to Moscow, has opened a joint investigation with Russia. Its prime minister, Osama Hamad, has asked the UN to investigate suspicions that the drones were launched from western Libya, which is controlled by the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli. Libya's coast is along Russia's shipping route to Asia, with tankers loading at Primorsk and Ust-Luga in the Baltic and at Novorossiysk on the Black Sea before crossing the Mediterranean to the Suez Canal. The Baltic ports alone typically supply 60% to 70% of the Russian crude shipped to India, according to Kpler data cited by ThePrint . Ukrainian drones have struck Russian energy cargoes on this route before. An official with Ukraine's SBU security service said Ukraine hit the empty shadow-fleet tanker Qendil off Libya in December last year. In March, Russia blamed Ukrainian naval drones launched from the Libyan coast for an attack on the Arctic Metagaz , an LNG carrier hauling more than 60,000 tons of gas from Murmansk to Egypt that sank about 130 nautical miles north of Sirte. Kyiv has not claimed that attack, and two Libyan officials told AP in April that Ukrainian forces operate from western Libya under a covert deal. Qatar, the world’s second-largest LNG exporter before the Iran war, has struggled to ship LNG carriers through the Strait of Hormuz, and gas flows have recovered only slightly, especially compared to the crude flows out of the Persian Gulf and the chokepoint. The Strait of Hormuz crisis hasn’t allowed many Qatari LNG cargoes to transit Hormuz since March. Like all other Asian importers, South Korea, the world’s third-largest LNG buyer after China and Japan, has been hit by the Middle East crisis and the lack of Qatari LNG supply. Soaring spot LNG prices for supply not needing the Strait of Hormuz have made running gas-fired plants uneconomical compared to coal. “In the short term, we are in a situation where we must somehow reduce LNG demand,” Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Kim Sungwhan told Bloomberg last month. Looking beyond the current Hormuz constraints, Kim Jung-kwan, South Korea’s Minister of Trade, Industry and Resources, on Monday met with Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Seoul, and asked for priority access to Qatar’s gas for Korea when Qatari LNG production and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz return to normal. title: Copper rout threatens Chile’s budget recovery hopes
summary: Falling metal prices, rising fuel subsidies and weak growth put President Kast's fiscal targets and credit standing at risk.
body: Falling metal prices, rising fuel subsidies and weak growth put President Kast's fiscal targets and credit standing at risk. President José Antonio Kast with Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas. ( Photo by Marcelo Segura. Courtesy of Chile’s government . ) Chile’s copper price slump is threatening President José Antonio Kast’s efforts to rein in the country’s fiscal deficit as rising fuel subsidies and weaker-than-expected economic growth strain government finances. Copper, which accounts for about half of Chile’s exports and a substantial share of government revenue, fell about 10% in New York last week. The decline pushed prices more than 20% below their record closing high on Sept. 9, briefly sending the metal into a bear market before a sharp rebound on Monday . “Persistently high oil prices and declining copper prices are an unwelcome combination for Chile, particularly at a time when economic growth remains sluggish,” William Snead, a strategist at BBVA, told Bloomberg News. “The country faces potential pressure on fiscal revenues, external accounts and domestic economic activity.” The reversal threatens a key source of funding for Latin America’s largest copper producer just as Kast faces mounting pressure to deliver on campaign promises to accelerate growth, restore fiscal discipline and balance the budget before his term ends. The government agreed this month to increase fuel subsidies following protests by truck drivers, adding to spending pressures. Separate economic data showed gross domestic product contracted more than expected in the third quarter. Kast, who took office March 11 , had already provided few updates on his pledge to cut $6 billion in spending within 18 months. His administration also abandoned a target to eliminate the structural budget deficit by 2030, raising questions about how it will consolidate public finances without the benefit of elevated copper prices. Copper prices nearly doubled in the three years through September, supported partly by investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence and the metal’s widespread use in data centres, power grids and electrical infrastructure. That momentum has since faded amid a broader selloff in AI-linked investments, leaving copper trading below its level when Kast assumed office. The retreat could significantly weaken government receipts after mining revenues helped improve Chile’s fiscal position earlier this year. Revenue from private mining companies rose 45% in real terms to 5.89 trillion pesos ($5.9 billion) during the first nine months of 2026, according to government figures . Transfers from state-owned copper producer Codelco increased 30% to 1.74 trillion pesos. Together, those sources accounted for 13% of government income during the period, helping narrow the budget deficit to 0.9% of GDP. The financial pressures come as Kast’s administration considers expanding private-sector involvement in state-owned Codelco. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz earlier this month left open the possibility of private investors eventually acquiring a minority stake, although he said the timing was not right. Days later, Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas said Chile was considering legislative changes to allow private companies to participate in some Codelco deposits or partner on infrastructure and processing facilities. The proposals have drawn criticism from the Socialist Party, unions and opposition lawmakers, who accuse the administration of overstating Codelco’s difficulties to build support for asset sales or greater private participation. The government and Codelco’s leadership reject those allegations. Lower copper prices could erode that contribution while the administration absorbs additional costs from its agreement with truck drivers. The fuel subsidy measures are expected to cost 279 billion pesos this year and another 523 billion pesos in 2027, according to legislative documents . title: Namib Minerals pours first gold at historic Redwing gold mine
summary: The mine in eastern Zimbabwe has been going through a phased restart, getting ready to restart commercial production.
body: The mine in eastern Zimbabwe has been going through a phased restart, getting ready to restart commercial production. Namib Minerals (Nasdaq: NAMM) has poured first gold at its century-old Redwing mine in eastern Zimbabwe, marking a return to commercial production after a seven-year hiatus. The company said the milestone comes after mine infrastructure and processing facilities were rehabilitated and recommissioned. Redwing historically produced about 650,000 ounces of gold between 1981 and 2023. “First gold is the beginning of the next phase, not the end of the job. Our focus now is to establish consistent, reliable production, demonstrate the operating performance of the mine and execute the planned ramp-up,” Namib CEO Tulani Sikwila said in a statement. Namib Minerals aims to build a combined annual production of 300,000 ounces in the long-term between the Redwing, How mine and Mazowe mine, still subject to technical studies, permitting and financing. The company expects to spend $300 million on mine restarts, Reuters reported. The Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) is fully funded with a conclusion expected in the first quarter of 2027, followed by resource definition drilling, the company said. Shares in Namib Minerals were slightly down 2.29% to $0.6 apiece by mid-day Monday in New York, valuing the company at $33.7 million. Namib Minerals said it is planning a staged ramp up, first trying to establish a reliable production record and stable mining and processing rhythm. The company expects to increase mining and processing through the installation and commissioning of a higher capacity winder. It said it targets to increase ore processing and gold production in 2027, depending on operating conditions. “Our ambition is to build a much larger African gold and critical metals business through operational delivery, disciplined capital allocation and responsible development,” Sikwila added. Namib Minerals already owns and operates the How mine in Bulawayo, which produced 25,000 ounces of gold in 2025. With Redwing’s restart, the company now becomes a multi-asset producer.

title: Canadian Copper sees expansion opportunites in New Brunswick
summary: Broad copper intervals found west of Murray Brook in New Brunswick may expand ore processing plans at Caribou mill.
body: Broad copper intervals found west of Murray Brook in New Brunswick may expand ore processing plans at Caribou mill. Canadian Copper (CSE: CCI) has reported broad copper-bearing drill intervals west of its Murray Brook deposit in New Brunswick, highlighting potential expansion opportunities as it advances plans to process the ore at the nearby Caribou mill. Hole MB26-06 cut 54.55 metres grading 0.80% copper from 29.45 metres downhole, including 33.15 metres at 1.14% copper, Canadian Copper said Monday in a statement . Hole MB26-16 returned 40.15 metres at 0.86% copper from 79 metres downhole. Canadian Copper tested ground up to 50 metres west of the deposit boundary, about 60 km west of Bathurst. “The combination of broad mineralized intervals, good copper grades, and proximity to our planned mining operations creates an opportunity to potentially improve the project’s economics,” CEO Simon Quick said. Shares of Canadian Copper rose 13% to 44¢ in Monday afternoon on the Canadian Securities Exchange, valuing the company at about C$102 million ($71 million). They’ve ranged between 32¢ and 82¢ in the past year. Canadian Copper expects to release a feasibility study in late January on mining Murray Brook and trucking ore 13 km to Caribou. It rushed selected mineralized intervals to the lab and expects complete hole assays in February, subject to lab availability. The reported intervals are downhole lengths; true widths remain unknown. Further modelling and technical evaluation are needed before the new mineralization can enter a resource estimate or mine plan. Canadian Copper completed the Caribou acquisition on July 28. The purchase gives it an existing mill, tailings facilities and supporting infrastructure to combine with its wholly owned Murray Brook deposit. A May 2025 preliminary economic assessment outlined an open pit feeding Caribou at 3,300 tonnes a day over more than 13 years. It estimated initial capital costs of $64 million and an after-tax net present value of $171 million at a 7% discount rate, using a copper price of US$4.25 per pound. The feasibility study was initially scheduled for December, according to a statement released in May when Canadian Copper appointed its study team. Its Nov. 16 update moved the expected release to late January, subject to final engineering and cost estimates. The company also expects an environmental-assessment update in the first quarter of 2027. In earlier development plans, management envisaged starting work at Murray Brook in 2027 and processing ore in 2028. Those targets depended on environmental review, permits, financing and a development decision. Canadian Copper reported more than C$24 million in treasury on Nov. 16 after receiving about C$9.8 million from warrant exercises. It’s also pursuing project funding through streaming and debt arrangements and has continued discussions with Ottawa about potential critical-minerals support.

title: Copper price roars back from bear market as Nvidia’s Huang U-turn revives AI trade
summary: New York copper futures were still sliding minutes before the Nvidia announcement. Marex says the jury is out on whether the bottom is in.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers remarks as President Donald Trump looks on during an “Investing in America” event on April 30, 2025, at the White House. Credit: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian. Copper staged one of its biggest rallies of the year on Monday, bouncing out of the bear market it entered on Friday, after Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and set off a rush back into the artificial intelligence trades that have dragged the metal down all month. Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, jumped as much as 5.5% to $5.787 a pound and was trading at $5.762 ($12,703 a tonne) in early New York trade, up 5% on the day. Earlier in the session it had sunk to $5.408, the lowest since the end of March. The contract settled at $5.485 on Friday, down 9.9% on the week and 20.4% below the record settlement of $6.889 reached on September 9, confirming the bear market it had flirted with during the session. Monday’s rebound cuts the deficit to 16% and carries copper back above $5.63, where it ended 2025, for a gain of 2% this year. It is still down 11% in November. The turn was abrupt. December copper was drifting lower near $5.46 a pound minutes before the Nvidia statement landed, a little over half an hour ahead of Wall Street’s opening bell, and was more than 5% higher about half an hour later. Nvidia said its directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president and chief executive with immediate effect, 11 days after he resigned. His departure had rattled the metals demand story and deepened a selloff in AI shares that spilled into copper, which is used in data centre wiring and the power networks that feed them. Nvidia shares soared about 28% in early trading and the Nasdaq Composite was up about 6%. London had a rougher morning before the Huang news broke. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange opened higher, then fell as much as 1.7% to $11,948 a tonne, the lowest since March 24 and within $50 of a bear market of its own, measured from the September peak of $14,875. It was up 0.1% at $12,168 in official trading, Reuters reports. The benchmark lost 9% last week, the third-biggest weekly slump this decade according to Bloomberg, and has shed almost 14% in November. “The jury is still out as to whether we’ve seen the bottom,” Alastair Munro, senior base metals strategist at Marex, told Reuters, noting that trend-following funds were still selling. Gao Yin, an analyst at Shuohe Asset Management, told Bloomberg that “some copper bears are getting ready to exit” while others think the AI story has fundamentally changed and intend to stay aggressively short. Last week’s industry gathering in Shanghai turned bearish on weak Chinese demand and growing doubt that US President Donald Trump will impose tariffs on refined copper this year, Bloomberg reports. Sceptics also point out that AI-related consumption remains small next to copper’s use in power grids and the wider energy transition. The physical scramble in China is cooling from extreme levels. title: AngloGold to pay 40% premium for Sitka Gold stake
summary: The investment comes as Sitka awaits assays from 82 holes totalling about 27,000 metres across six targets.
body: The investment comes as Sitka awaits assays from 82 holes totalling about 27,000 metres across six targets. A view of the RC project area in the Yukon. Credit: Sitka Gold AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU; JSE: ANG) has agreed to invest at least $72.8 million (US$50.8 million) for a 15% stake in Sitka Gold (TSXV: SIG; US-OTC: SITKF) as the Yukon explorer awaits results from nearly half of this year’s drilling at RC Gold. AngloGold will pay 95¢ a share, compared with Sitka’s Friday close of 68¢. Sitka rose 18% to 80¢ in Toronto by midday Monday, valuing the company at about $347 million. The project lies about 365 km northwest of Whitehorse. “This substantial investment by one of the world’s largest gold producers is a major validator for both the RC gold project and the company,” Sitka CEO Cor Coe said in a release. “With our 60,000-metre drill program now complete and a strengthened treasury, we look forward to working alongside AngloGold Ashanti’s industry-leading technical teams and drawing on their mine-building experience as we continue to develop this wide-open gold system.” Sitka will retain full ownership of RC Gold. At closing, AngloGold would gain the right to nominate a Sitka director and preferential rights on certain transactions involving the project. The two companies would also form a technical committee to discuss its development. Sitka is awaiting assays from 82 holes totalling about 27,000 metres across six targets, including the Blackjack, Eiger and Rhosgobel deposits. Blackjack holds 39.96 million indicated tonnes grading 1.01 grams gold per tonne for 1.29 million oz., according to a January 2025 estimate. A February 2026 update put the total across all three deposits at 167.4 million inferred tonnes grading 0.72 gram gold per tonne for 3.83 million ounces. Rhosgobel, where Sitka reported its first drill results in 2024, accounts for 2.25 million of those inferred ounces. Sitka expects to raise $83.3 million to $101.6 million in all. AngloGold’s investment could reach $75.5 million if other shareholders exercise their rights to participate and the producer buys more shares to maintain its 15% stake. The offering includes up to 26.3 million flow-through shares at $1.35 each. Sitka plans to spend those proceeds on exploration at RC Gold by the end of 2027 and expects the financing to close in December, subject to TSX Venture Exchange approval.

title: Panama, First Quantum begin talks on giant copper mine’s reopening
summary: First Quantum accepted five conditions from the government for reopening negotiations, officials announced after Monday's meeting.
body: First Quantum accepted five conditions from the government for reopening negotiations, officials announced after Monday's meeting. Cobre Panama copper mine was shut down in November 2023. ( Image courtesy of Cobre Panama. ) Panama and First Quantum Minerals (TSX: FM) opened formal negotiations Monday over the future of the Cobre Panama copper mine, a former economic powerhouse shuttered since 2023 following nationwide protests and a Supreme Court ruling that invalidated its operating contract. Trade and Industry Minister Julio Moltó leads the government’s first official meeting with representatives of the Canadian miner’s local subsidiary, Minera Panamá. The talks follow President José Raúl Mulino’s announcement last week that his administration is ready to seek a resolution to the dispute. First Quantum agreed to five conditions set by Panama’s government for negotiations over a potential reopening, authorities said following Monday’s meeting. The conditions include recognizing Panama’s ownership of its mineral resources, creating more jobs for Panamanians, meeting the highest environmental standards and respecting the country’s sovereignty, Constitution and laws. The Canadian miner said it reiterated its willingness to participate “constructively and transparently in the formal discussions led by the Government of Panama, with full respect for Panama’s sovereignty and the public participation process.” The government announced the agreement following the meeting, describing the discussions as the start of a “transparent and participatory” process that will consider public input before any final decision. First Quantum did not comment on the talks. First Quantum shares rose 6.2% in Toronto on Monday morning to C$27.77 a piece, giving the company a market capitalization of C$23.12 billion ($16 billion). The negotiations could determine when First Quantum may eventually resume mining at an operation that once generated about 40% of its revenue. They also present a test for Panama’s government as it weighs the economic benefits of restoring copper production against constitutional restrictions, environmental obligations and public opposition that forced the mine’s closure. The government’s negotiating team includes representatives from the ministries of Trade and Industries, Economy and Finance, and Environment, working under guidelines established by the executive branch. Economy and Finance Minister Felipe Chapman confirmed that officials would evaluate the available alternatives to determine which best serves Panama’s interests. Moltó said the government expects to be in a position to provide an update by the first quarter of 2027, provided the conditions for an agreement are met. “We identify the right legal framework that complies with the Constitution, conduct consultations and discussions with the public, and receive the public’s information and feedback through the Escazú mechanism,” Moltó said in an interview with Telemetro . “We will, of course, keep the public informed of our progress, as we have throughout this process.” Despite First Quantum’s acceptance of the negotiating conditions , the government has yet to authorize a restart of mining operations. Mulino has also insisted that any settlement include the termination of international arbitration proceedings against Panama. If permanent closure is chosen, First Quantum would have to finance an orderly, verifiable and definitive shutdown without extensions. The president has pledged to make the terms of any agreement public once negotiations conclude. A three-minister government commission recommended a path toward restarting Cobre Panama in September, following an independent audit by Swiss consultants and an assessment of the operation’s economic, environmental and legal implications. First Mining Gold (TSX: FF; US-OTC: FFMGF) has received Ontario’s environmental-assessment approval for the Springpole gold project in northwestern Ontario as it looks to finance a proposed $1.1 billion (C$1.6 billion) open-pit operation. The stock soared. Ontario Environment Minister Todd McCarthy approved the assessment for the project 110 km northeast of Red Lake, First Mining announced Monday . Ottawa had approved the project on June 30. The company is targeting completion of a feasibility study and project financing in 2027, ahead of a construction decision in 2028. Further project permits and authorizations are still required. “While provincial approval was anticipated, its receipt is a major de-risking milestone and materially improves visibility toward feasibility, financing and construction and is consistent with our development assumptions,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Alex Terentiew said. When considering formalized agreements in place with local First Nations communities, “Springpole has now secured the principal environmental and social approvals required to advance toward a development decision,” Terentiew added. “Secondary permits, financing and board approval remain outstanding, but the key permitting risk underpinning our thesis has now been removed.” First Mining shares jumped 9.4% to 58¢ Monday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$864 million ($600 million). They’ve traded between 30.5¢ and 98¢ over the past year. Investor focus will now shift to execution instead of environmental assessment, Terentiew said. Part of the deposit lies beneath Springpole Lake. First Mining plans to build two dykes and drain part of the lake to reach the ore. Under federal conditions, it must establish at least one Indigenous environmental committee before construction. The committees will help monitor water quality and measures to protect caribou. “This land will always be home to our people long after the Springpole Project has ended,” Lac Seul First Nation Chief Clifford Bull said in August, when his nation and Cat Lake First Nation signed a benefits agreement with the company. First Mining held C$81 million ($56.3 million) in cash and marketable securities at Sept. 30 after raising gross proceeds of C$57.5 million in a September share sale. The company plans an 18-km all-weather access road, a construction camp and a power connection. It already has permits for a winter road to resupply its existing camp. Springpole could produce 330,000 payable oz. gold a year in its first five years and average 281,000 oz. over a 9.4-year mine life, First Mining estimated in its 2025 prefeasibility study. At a gold price of $3,100 per oz., the project had an after-tax net present value of $2.1 billion at a 5% discount rate and a 41% internal rate of return. Initial capital costs were estimated at $1.1 billion. Cat Lake and Lac Seul conducted their own impact assessment before reaching an August agreement to share in the project’s financial benefits. First Mining also signed a separate agreement with Slate Falls Nation that month.

title: Ground View Pakistan: Beyond Reko Diq, today
summary: A reporting trip to Islamabad reveals mineral opportunities across Pakistan’s north, even as its flagship copper project slows.
body: A reporting trip to Islamabad reveals mineral opportunities across Pakistan’s north, even as its flagship copper project slows. Pakistan’s mineral investment ambitions extend well beyond the giant Reko Diq copper-gold project, with emerging exploration and processing opportunities offering a chance to build an industry before the country’s flagship mine begins production. That was my clearest takeaway from the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF) in Islamabad, where the theme, “Beyond Reko Diq,” largely focused on what might follow the mine once it enters production. After speaking with explorers, processors, government officials, financiers and students, I came away convinced that the opportunities are not necessarily sequential. “Beyond Reko Diq, today” would have been a more fitting theme. The distinction matters because Pakistan has concentrated much of its mining investment strategy on a single development whose timeline remains uncertain. Barrick’s decision to slow development and extend its review until mid-2027 underscores the risks of relying so heavily on one project. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told me that Reko Diq’s first year of production had been expected to equal roughly 10% of Pakistan’s current goods exports. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the country could point to just “one example” of a major international miner operating there, although he hoped to see four or five within two years. The legal protections supporting foreign investment also illustrate that dependence. Reko Diq required project-specific legislation, raising questions about whether smaller developers can secure comparable assurances without negotiating their own arrangements. The investment forum revealed a much broader mineral landscape than the copper-gold deposits of Balochistan that originally drew me to Pakistan. Waleed Ahmed Vohra of Ark Metals described using satellite imagery and hyperspectral analysis to narrow a lithium exploration search across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan from 150,000 sq. km to roughly 400 sq. km considered highly prospective. Liaqat Ali Sultan, who operates a mineral processing business in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, discussed opportunities involving antimony, tungsten and rare earths in placer black sands. His operation had also attracted a visit from a US consul general, suggesting growing international interest in the region’s mineral potential. Punjab’s chief minister announced the province’s first dedicated mineral processing zone, signalling ambitions to capture more value from domestic resources. At a university earth sciences department, a doctoral student from northern Pakistan described mineral-rich areas that remain largely unexplored. These conversations suggested an industry with multiple possible starting points rather than a development pipeline waiting for Reko Diq. Smaller, higher-grade deposits could offer a practical route to establishing Pakistan’s mining credentials. They may require less upfront capital, more manageable infrastructure and processing facilities better suited to the financing available in an emerging industry. That matters because lenders generally want evidence of reliable feedstock before financing smelters and refineries, while international investors look for operating records that demonstrate a jurisdiction can deliver. Pakistan could begin establishing that credibility through smaller operations while its largest development advances. The northern regions nevertheless present substantial challenges, and enthusiasm for their mineral potential should not be confused with evidence of commercially viable deposits. Much of the exploration excitement rests on surface samples rather than defined mineral resources. Vohra cautioned that mining economics depend on the scale and continuity of mineralization, not simply spectacular grades in isolated samples. summary: Mining giant targets 650,000 tonnes annually by 2040, but high costs, water shortages and technical hurdles pose challenges.
body: Mining giant targets 650,000 tonnes annually by 2040, but high costs, water shortages and technical hurdles pose challenges. BHP's Olympic Dam mining and smelting complex in South Australia. ( Image courtesy of BHP. ) BHP (ASX, LON: BHP) plans to invest up to $17.4 billion to double copper production in South Australia by 2040, betting on rising demand for the metal despite a history of costly setbacks in the region. The world’s largest miner expects to spend between $13.6 billion and $17.4 billion to lift annual output to about 650,000 tonnes from its Copper South Australia operations, with a final investment decision expected in the first half of 2027. The expansion would tap what BHP describes as the world’s richest copper-bearing region outside Chile. “We start from a strong position as the world’s largest copper producer, with a sector-leading growth pathway that can be funded from existing copper cash flows,” Geraldine Slattery, BHP’s head of Australian operations, told investors during a site tour . The investment would strengthen copper’s growing importance to BHP as electrification, artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure drive demand. The metal generated more value for the miner than iron ore, its traditional mainstay, for the first time in fiscal 2026. BHP expects global copper demand to rise 30% by 2040 to more than 45 million tonnes annually. Its Australian expansion would contribute about a third of the company’s planned production growth through 2035, Slattery said. The strategy brings together the Olympic Dam mine and smelting complex, the Ankata deposit and assets acquired through BHP’s A$9.6 billion takeover of OZ Minerals in 2023. BHP expects its South Australian operations to rival its stake in Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, in production by 2040. The expansion supports its ambition to produce 2 million tonnes of copper annually by the mid-2030s, or 2.5 million tonnes including byproducts. The miner is also pursuing growth in Chile, where it has operated for more than three decades. It has outlined plans to spend up to $14 billion expanding its copper operations there , targeting an additional 430,000 to 540,000 tonnes of annual production while evaluating new projects. BHP’s ambitions face considerable technical and financial hurdles in South Australia, where the company has twice abandoned development plans in previous decades because of high costs and weak commodity markets. Operational instability, complex metallurgy and limited water and power infrastructure have constrained performance, UBS analysts said in a note. The assets generated low single-digit returns on capital employed for years, reaching 10% only in fiscal 2026 amid record-high commodity prices, according to UBS. That history raises questions about whether BHP can deliver attractive returns on another multibillion-dollar investment. The company plans to use block caving, a bulk underground mining method, alongside two-stage smelting to reduce operating costs. The first phase targets annual copper production of 500,000 tonnes by 2035, with a projected internal rate of return of 14% to 17% and capital intensity of $18,000 to $23,000 per tonne of copper. The expansion would also increase production of other commodities. BHP plans to roughly double uranium processing capacity to between 5,000 and 6,000 tonnes annually while lifting gold output by 45% to more than 570,000 troy ounces a year. Securing enough water and electricity could prove as important as developing the ore deposits themselves. BHP’s operations lie within the Gawler Craton, a geological formation dating back roughly 2 billion years, in an increasingly arid region bordering Australia’s remote Outback. The miner currently draws water from the Great Artesian Basin, a practice that has raised concerns among traditional owners, including the Arabana people, about the long-term sustainability of the resource. title: Eldorado moves closer to production at Greek gold mine
summary: Four tailings filter presses are now operating at Skouries, with the company targeting year-end output.
body: Four tailings filter presses are now operating at Skouries, with the company targeting year-end output. Commercial production at Skouries is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. ( Image courtesy of Eldorado Gold. ) Eldorado Gold (TSX: ELD; NYSE: EGO) has brought all four required tailings filter presses into operation at its Skouries copper-gold mine in northern Greece, clearing a key requirement for commercial production by the end of 2026. The Canadian miner said the additional filtration capacity supports its ongoing ramp-up, with commercial production expected late this quarter. Four operating presses are needed to support commercial production from sulphide ore, while five are required to achieve nameplate throughput. “With four filter presses now operational, we have achieved another important milestone in the ramp-up of Skouries,” CEO Christian Milau said. The development brings Eldorado closer to transitioning Skouries from construction to commercial operations after years of setbacks. The mine recently produced its first copper-gold concentrate , marking an important step toward establishing a new source of both metals in Europe. The Skouries tailings filtration facility comprises six Metso filter presses, including five operating units and one installed spare. The spare provides operational flexibility and allows maintenance without reducing throughput. The remaining two presses are expected to become operational in early December, the company said , providing additional capacity and redundancy as processing rates increase. The mine’s ore stockpile now exceeds 4.6 million tonnes, enough to sustain more than seven months of planned processing throughput. Skouries is expected to produce about 140,000 oz. of gold and 67 million lb. of copper annually from combined open-pit and underground operations. The European Commission granted Skouries strategic project status last month, potentially accelerating permitting and improving access to financing as the mine ramps up production. Skouries is among 46 projects selected under the EU initiative to strengthen Europe’s access to critical raw materials. The designation provides for faster permitting and assistance in seeking public and private financing, but does not constitute a direct funding commitment from the Commission. Eldorado also expects to file an updated technical report for Skouries in the first quarter of 2027. It will incorporate a revised resource model and metal price assumptions, alongside updated production forecasts, operating costs and capital estimates reflecting the transition from development to operations.

summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was becoming the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia— until he reversed course
body: For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China. For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang 's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to China. They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington. By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump 's urging. Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang. Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk. A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes. "Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival. Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes. "Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift. Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race. But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal . He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously." But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week. Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said. Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory. "I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable." Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS. Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. According to Arnott, strong buying activity during the earlier price rally may have created additional selling pressure once gold began losing value.
