body: Bsinews.id, Jakarta , Global copper markets are experiencing sharply different conditions as financial selling pushes London prices lower while dwindling inventories create a supply squeeze in Shanghai. The contrasting developments, reported by Reuters columnist Andy Home on November 20, 2026, reflect weakening investment sentiment, China's tight domestic supply and uncertainty surrounding potential US import tariffs. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) dropped 6% to $12,379.50 per metric ton on Wednesday, reaching its lowest level in seven months. The decline followed heavy selling by investment funds as enthusiasm for artificial intelligence weakened, the US dollar strengthened and economic uncertainty increased. Tin experienced similar pressure, falling to an eight-month low of $41,035 per ton. Both metals had previously benefited from growing expectations of artificial intelligence infrastructure investment, particularly demand from data centers. However, weaker expectations for AI investment have increased concerns about industrial demand. Citi analysts estimated that global copper consumption grew by just 0.8% year-on-year in August, with weak domestic consumption in China contributing significantly to the slowdown. Despite softer demand, China's copper market experienced an extraordinary shortage of deliverable metal during the November Shanghai Futures Exchange (ShFE) contract expiry. The November copper contract surged more than 9% to 118,060 yuan per ton on Monday, reaching an unprecedented squeeze as available inventories proved insufficient to cover outstanding delivery commitments. At one stage, its premium over the December contract exceeded 10,000 yuan per ton. According to ShFE inventory figures, deliverable stocks declined from a March peak of 433,458 tons to just 27,642 tons. Only 2,270 tons were available for settlement of November contracts. Physical market indicators also demonstrate the shortage. Domestic copper premiums have increased, while the Yangshan premium, assessed by Shanghai Metals Market, climbed to a record $360 per ton above the LME price. China's refined copper production has also faced pressure from tight raw material availability. According to the Reuters report, domestic output is expected to record its slowest growth in decades, while refined copper imports declined 12.5% year-on-year during the first nine months of 2026. The supply imbalance has intensified competition between China and the United States, where expectations of import tariffs previously encouraged traders to direct copper shipments toward American warehouses. According to the World Bureau of Metal Statistics, US copper imports increased 80% year-on-year to 1.64 million tons in 2025. Imports subsequently rose another 10% to 1.31 million tons during the first eight months of 2026. This movement has also affected inventories registered with the LME. Metal held under LME warrants increased from less than 100,000 tons in August to 291,925 tons, largely reflecting deliveries into US ports. Traders found it increasingly attractive to register copper with the LME rather than clear it through customs and deliver it to warehouses associated with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME). Meanwhile, the CME copper premium has contracted considerably. body: Wall Street's view of the oil market is undergoing a marked shift. Bernstein's latest crude oil outlook report states bluntly that global supply growth will once again outpace demand, with the oil market likely falling back into oversupply over the next three years. It forecasts Brent crude averaging $80 a barrel (about NT$2,600) in 2027, then sliding to $75 (about NT$2,500) in 2028. The report, written by analyst Neil Beveridge and others, amounts to a bombshell for an oil market that was once tight this year. During the outbreak of the US-Iran War this year, the market briefly faced a supply gap of about 1.3 million barrels per day, and only the release of strategic reserves by the OECD and several major economies kept a lid on prices. The report argues that this delicate balance, propped up by drawing down inventories, will reverse sharply in 2027. The report estimates that with Persian Gulf exports fully recovering and production capacity from non-OPEC oil producers gradually coming online, the market will be oversupplied by more than 2.5 million barrels per day in 2027, and the loose conditions could persist through 2029. Notably, Bernstein is not alone in its bearish oil price view. Goldman Sachs earlier also projected that global crude output would exceed demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027, with Brent falling to around $78 (about NT$2,600) as risk premiums fade. International Energy Agency (IEA) statistics likewise point to rebalancing, with global output last month exceeding consumption by nearly 2 million barrels per day. However, the report stresses that oil prices may not fall off a cliff. Bernstein estimates that although the total surplus in 2027 could approach 1 billion barrels, a considerable portion will be absorbed by countries rebuilding strategic reserves and by floating storage, forming a "giant sponge" that cushions the impact on the spot market. What really worries analysts is the ebbing of the geopolitical premium. Brent crude climbed from this year's lows all the way above $90 (about NT$3,000), a rally that largely reflected expectations of a wider war; once fundamentals regain control of pricing, that premium could be squeezed out quickly. The report warns that investors must re-examine their positioning logic, including whether sectors previously suppressed by high oil prices are set for a reversal and how to deploy hedging positions in advance. Timing, though, is always the hard part. Earlier this month, the oil market quickly priced in the political deadlock following the US midterm election results, with Brent futures plunging more than 16% in a week, the biggest weekly drop since 2020; the market then quickly restored the premium and prices rebounded on fears of a US military strike on Iran. This back-and-forth tug-of-war is the best depiction of the current oil market. Deutsche Bank, meanwhile, believes the international oil market may be in for a prolonged standoff. On one hand, the IEA estimates the surplus will reach 4.5 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2027; on the other, supply-side disruptions such as restricted navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and sudden shutdowns at Libyan oil fields could still ignite short-term rallies at any time. From an industry perspective, if the oversupply scenario materializes in 2027, cost pressures on downstream sectors such as aviation, logistics and chemicals should ease markedly, and market funds may shift from direct bets on crude toward real-economy industries that benefit from lower oil prices.
